summary: Describes an LDAP control and schema for retrieving digitally signed directory information, so changes to each entry can be kept in a signed journal. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A directory keeps a signed diary of every change, so later you can check that nobody altered the entries.

subtitle: Digital signatures on LDAP directory changes to create an audit trail.

tldr.problem: LDAP directory servers store information that changes over time, but there is no standard way to record who made each change and verify that changes have not been tampered with.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC defines LDAP controls that allow operations to include digital signatures, and a schema for storing those signatures as an audit trail on each directory entry.
tldr.outcome: Directory administrators can create a signed journal of all changes to sensitive entries, so later they can verify the complete history and detect tampering.

today: RFC 2649 remains Experimental and has not been widely deployed. Modern LDAP deployments typically rely on TLS for connection security and the underlying directory server's access control and logging for audit trails rather than application-level signed operations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
LDAP is the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, used to store and retrieve information from centralized directories (like user accounts and contact information). This RFC defines how to add digital signatures to LDAP operations so that a complete audit trail is created and stored in the directory itself.

The core idea is that when an LDAP client creates, modifies, or deletes an entry, it can include a SignedOperation control with a digital signature (created with the client's private key) or a request for the server to sign the operation on its behalf. The server records this signature in the directory entry itself as part of a Changes attribute, creating a permanent journal of who did what and when.

This allows administrators to verify the source and integrity of directory information later: they can check the signature on each change and confirm that the entry has not been secretly modified.
sections.eli5: Every time someone changes a file in the directory, a digital signature proves who did it. The signatures pile up as a permanent record.

sections.title: Signed Directory Operations
sections.content:
The SignedOperation control (OID 1.2.840.113549.6.0.0) can be included in an LDAP request to indicate that the operation should be signed. The control contains one of two choices: signByServer (NULL, requesting the server to sign the operation) or signatureIncluded (an S/MIME message containing the client's signature).

When a client includes a signature, it first builds the LDAP message without the control, computes an S/MIME signature over that message, then includes the signature in a new SignedOperation control in a second message with the same operation.

The signature is recorded in the directory entry in a signedAuditTrail object, which contains a Changes attribute. The Changes attribute is a sequence of entries, each with a sequence number and the signed operation. Sequence number 0 always represents the initial state of the entry; subsequent numbers record changes in order.

The control can be marked CRITICAL. If it is critical and the server understands it, the server must record the signature. If the server cannot verify the signature and wishes to reject the operation, it returns an error code.
sections.eli5: You sign your change with your key, or ask the server to sign it for you. Either way, the signature goes into the directory so everyone can see the audit trail.

sections.title: Handling Deletes
sections.content:
Deleting a directory entry presents a problem: after the entry is deleted, there is no entry in the directory to hold the audit trail of changes. To solve this, the RFC defines a zombieObject object class. When an entry is deleted with a signed operation, the server creates a zombie object in its place, containing all the Changes attributes from the original entry plus the signature of the delete operation itself.

The zombie object has a generated common name (CN) synthesized by the server (it may not match the original entry's name). The zombie contains an OriginalObject attribute that holds an LDAP URL pointing to where the original entry was located.

This allows auditors to reconstruct the complete history of a deleted entry by examining the zombie object, confirming that the deletion was signed and by whom.
sections.eli5: When you delete a file, a ghost file stays behind with all the signatures, so you can still see who deleted it and when.

sections.title: Signing Search Results
sections.content:
A second control, DemandSignedResult (OID 1.2.840.113549.6.0.1), allows a client to request that the server sign the results of a search query. The control contains a boolean value: TRUE means sign the results, FALSE means do not sign them.

If the server supports this control and agrees to sign results, it returns the normal search results along with a SignedResult control (OID 1.2.840.113549.6.0.2) in the response, containing an S/MIME pkcs-7 signature over the entire LDAPResult.

Some servers may be configured to always sign their operations and results. Such a server will always include the SignedResult control unless explicitly told not to by the client's control.

Because SignedResult is not marked as CRITICAL, clients are allowed to ignore it if they do not support signature verification.
sections.eli5: You can ask the directory server to prove that the answers it gave you are genuine, by signing them.

sections.title: Security and Limitations
sections.content:
The main purpose of this mechanism is to provide an audit trail, not to guarantee the security of the initial LDAP connection. The underlying network connection should use TLS or another secure protocol to prevent tampering in transit.

Although the server may verify signatures when it receives them, clients should independently verify signatures when retrieving audit trail information. They should also check whether the signing certificate has been revoked or the private key compromised by consulting the issuing certification authorities.

The document explicitly disclaims providing a guarantee of origin and integrity for all LDAP operations; that service is better provided by TLS. This specification is designed to provide a persistent audit trail and the ability to verify changes after the fact, not to prevent tampering during transmission.

If any of the signature controls are supported by an LDAP server, the server must make its certificate available in the userCertificate attribute of the root DSE object so clients can verify server-signed operations.
sections.eli5: The signatures prove who made changes, but you still need TLS or encryption for the actual network connection. Verifying the signatures later is the client's job.
